'''''Symphoricarpos''''' is a small genus of about 15 [[species]] of [[deciduous]] [[shrub]]s in the family [[Caprifoliaceae]]. With the exception of the Chinese coralberry, ''[[Symphoricarpos sinensis|S. sinensis]]'', which is indigenous to western China, all species are native to [[North America|North]] and [[Central America]]. The name of the genus is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] words {{lang|grc|συμφορεῖν}} ({{grc-tr|συμφορεῖν}}), meaning "to bear together", and {{lang|grc|καρπός}} ({{grc-tr|καρπός}}), meaning "fruit". It refers to the closely packed clusters of berries the species produces.<ref name="NYBG">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KeGzp-YXrPYC |first=Thomas H. |last=Everett |title=The New York Botanical Garden Illustrated Encyclopedia of Horticulture |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-8240-7240-7 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |page=3271}}</ref> Species in the genus are known by several [[Common name|common names]], including '''snowberry''', '''waxberry''' and '''ghostberry'''.

Snowberry is a resilient plant able to withstand a variety of conditions. Their deep roots allow them to survive dry seasons,  and they have been known to grow in a variety of soil types such as light sandy soil, medium loamy soil and heavier clay soil.<ref name=":0" /> Snowberry plants are most commonly found low-to mid elevations, in forests, dry or moist openings, rocky hillsides or near riverbanks and streams.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=''Symphoricarpos'' |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Symphoricarpos+albus+laevigatus|website=Plants For A Future}}</ref> Snowberry plants are also able to grow in a wide range of acidic and basic [[pH]]s and sunlight conditions.<ref name=":0" />

==Description==
''Symphoricarpos'' [[leaf|leaves]] are {{convert|1.5|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, rounded, entire or with one or two lobes at the base.<ref name=USDA>{{Cite web |last=Favorite|first= Jammie|editor= Lincoln M. Moore |year=2008|title= Plant fact sheet for snowberry [''Symphoricarpos albus'' (L.) Blake.]|publisher= USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service|location= National Plant Data Center, Greensboro, NC 27401 |url=https://plants.usda.gov/documentlibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_syal.pdf}}</ref> The [[flower]]s are small, greenish-white to pink, in small clusters of 5–15 together in most species, solitary or in pairs in some (e.g. ''S. microphyllus''). The [[fruit]] is conspicuous, {{convert|1|–|2|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter, soft, varying from white (e.g. ''S. albus'') to pink (''[[Symphoricarpos microphyllus|S. microphyllus]]'') to red (''[[Symphoricarpos orbiculatus|S. orbiculatus]]'') and in one species (''[[Symphoricarpos sinensis|S. sinensis]]''), blackish purple. When the white berries are broken open, the interior looks like fine, sparkling granular snow. The flesh is spongy and contains two 2–5 mm long, whitish stone seeds. The seeds, which contain endosperm and a small embryo, are egg-shaped and more or less flattened. They have a very tough, hard, impermeable covering, and so are very hard to germinate and may lie dormant for up to ten years.

The white berries create a cracking sound when they are stepped into firm ground.

==Ecology==
Snowberry is a [[Hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] species meaning it contains both male and female reproductive organs.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Snowberry|url=http://www.preciousprairieplants.com/snowberry.html|access-date=2021-02-19|website=Precious Prairie Plants}}</ref> It has the ability to grow via seeds but typically reproduces by releasing [[Shoot (botany)|shoots]] from a [[rhizome]]. This method of shoot dispersal allows snowberry to grow in dense populations of bushes and trees.<ref name=":1" /> Snowberry plants also tend to use a reproductive method called layering in which the plant's vertical stems will wilt and droop until they touch surrounding soil.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Scasta|first1=John Derek |last2=Engle|first2=David M. |last3=Harr|first3=Ryan N. |last4=Debinski|first4=Diane M. |date=2014-12-24 |title=Fire induced reproductive mechanisms of a ''Symphoricarpos'' (Caprifoliaceae) shrub after dormant season burning |url= |journal=Botanical Studies |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=80 |doi=10.1186/s40529-014-0080-4 |issn=1999-3110 |pmc=5432769 |pmid=28510959 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2014BotSt..55...80S }}</ref> Upon making contact with soil, roots will begin to form. Snowberry plants are resilient and studies have proved they are able to tolerate dormant [[Wildfire|seasonal fires]]. These fires actually encourage the snowberry plant's layering reproductive method, as the regeneration of new plants results in an increased number of [[Plant stem|stems]] and therefore more opportunities for layering to occur.<ref name=":2" />

Common snowberry (''[[Symphoricarpos albus|S. albus]]'') is a resilient plant that thrives in dry woodland conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Resources |first=University of California, Division of Agriculture and Natural |title=Waterwise Plants |url=https://mgsantaclara.ucanr.edu/garden-help/water-wise-plants/?uid=101&ds=833 |access-date=2024-10-23 |website=mgsantaclara.ucanr.edu |language=en-US}}</ref> Its berries ripen during fall and last through winter, making it an important winter food source for [[quail]] and [[grouse]]. However, the berries are considered poisonous to humans. The berries contain the [[isoquinoline]] [[alkaloid]] [[chelidonine]], as well as other alkaloids. Ingesting the berries causes mild symptoms of vomiting, dizziness, and slight [[sedation]] in children.

==Cultivation==
Common snowberry is a popular [[ornamental plant|ornamental shrub]] in [[garden]]s, grown for its decorative white fruit and [[wildlife garden]]ing. It is also a useful landscaping plant due to its extreme versatility—tolerating sun, shade, heat, cold, drought, and inundation.

==Medicinal uses==
Due to their low [[saponin]] content, snowberry was a common medicinal treatment used by several North American Indigenous tribes. Snowberry contains low concentrations of saponins, which are anti-[[carcinogen]]ic and anti-[[inflammation|inflammatory]].<ref name=":3">{{Citation |last=Savage|first=G. P. |date=2016 |title=Saponins☆ |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Food and Health |pages=714–716 |editor-last=Caballero |editor-first=Benjamin |place=Oxford |publisher=Academic Press |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-384947-2.00610-3 |isbn=978-0-12-384953-3 |editor2-last=Finglas |editor2-first=Paul M. |editor3-last=Toldrá |editor3-first=Fidel}}</ref> Saponins have also been proven to help with immune function and decrease [[cholesterol]].<ref name=":3" /> Saponins can be extremely toxic if consumed in excess,<ref name=":3" /> but are typically applied externally or consumed in concentrations too low to inflict damage.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Moerman |first=Daniel E. |title=Native American ethnobotany |date=1998 |isbn=0-88192-453-9 |location=Portland, Oregon |publisher=Timber Press |oclc=38002531}}</ref> Its toxic effects can also be reduced through cooking.<ref name=USDA/>

The snowberry plant is known to be [[disinfectant]], [[laxative]], [[diuretic]] and has the ability to reduce fever.<ref name=":4" /> Native Americans found several uses for the snowberry plant. Snowberry leaves were chewed up and used in a [[poultice]] to treat external wounds.<ref name=":4" /> Its berries were used for a number of applications including as an eyewash, as an antiperspirant, a diarrhea remedy, and was also rubbed on the skin as a treatment for burns, rashes, warts, sores, cuts and other external wounds.<ref name=":4" /> Snowberry stems were boiled and their essence was extracted to be used for stomach problems, menstrual pain, and as a soap. Weaker dilutions were used for children, meanwhile stronger concentrations were used as a disinfectant to clean open sores.<ref name=":4" /> Snowberry bark was also boiled, its essence extracted and used to treat sexually transmitted diseases and urinary dysfunction issues. Its roots were commonly used in the treatment of fever, stomach ache, common cold, and even [[tuberculosis]].<ref name=":4" /> In California, the Coastal Miwok used pounded snowberry root to treat ailments such as the cold.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barrett 1, Gifford 2 |first=S.A. 1, E.W. 2 |date=1933 |title=Miwok Material Culture: Indian Life of the Yosemite Region (1933) |url=https://www.yosemite.ca.us/library/miwok_material_culture/medicines.html}}</ref>

Due to the content of saponins in the berries, some tribes of the Pacific Northwest used the crushed fruits to stun fish in lakes and rivers in order to facilitate the harvesting of fish. The saponins, which are not toxic to humans, interfere with oxygen absorption in the gills.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://nativeplantspnw.com/common-snowberry-symphoricarpos-albus/ |title=Common Snowberry, ''Symphoricarpos albus'' |website=nativeplantspnw.com. |date=27 February 2017 |access-date=25 August 2023}}</ref>

==Other uses==
In Ireland, children use the berries for play, bursting the berries close to each other's ears. The berries are known as "billy busters".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-08-16 |title=Out and About in Laois |url=https://www.laoispeople.ie/out-and-about-in-laois-2/ |access-date=2023-08-28 |website=Laois People |language=en-US}}</ref>
